p.t: Central banks in many advanced countries are unwinding their bond holdings purchased during phases of quantitative easing (QE). These Treasury sales, commonly known as quantitative tightening (QT), are expected to lower bond prices and raise long-term interest rates. Can this happen in a controlled manner symmetric to the QE phase? Would financial frictions that made QE effective backfire during QT and make it ineffective or even destructive? In this paper, we show that QT could be more than QE in reverse mode, because these policy actions shift the composition of the marginal investors in the Treasury market. We begin by documenting some new facts about investor composition during the past two QT episodes in 2017-19 and 2022-23. We classify typical financial intermediaries-brokers and dealers, banks, hedge funds-as the liquidity traders in this market, and we refer to the remaining market participants as the long-term bond investors. Consistent with the notion that liquidity traders are more attentive to the market, we find that they adjust their portfolio positions much more aggressively than domestic and foreign bond investors. In response to the Fed's sales of Treasury bonds, the liquidity traders expanded their Treasury holdings by 60% to 80% relative to their initial positions, whereas other investors responded by much less. As a result, the Treasury debt sold by the Fed was disproportionately absorbed by the liquidity traders. Does this change in investor composition matter for bond valuation and the effectiveness of QT? Indeed, QT was accompanied by a negative return on the long-term Treasury bond portfolio.

For example, from November 2021 to October 2023, the Bloomberg US Long Treasury Bond Index declined by 40%, an unusually large loss in the Treasury market which is traditionally regarded as safe and stable. However, this decline in Treasury prices could be driven by other factors such as economic fundamentals and monetary policy rates, which makes it difficult to interpret. Motivated by these observations, we develop a general equilibrium model to study how the interaction between these two investor classes affects bond valuation. We assume that long-term bond investors have a higher risk-taking capacity, which makes them the more efficient holders of the Treasury bonds. However, they face a portfolio adjustment cost, which prevents them from adjusting to their target portfolio instantly after shocks. In comparison, liquidity traders have a lower risk-taking capacity, but they can adjust their positions freely without transaction costs. As a result, they will be the first responders to fundamental or monetary shocks, and they charge a risk premium for providing this service. Our model highlights a new, dynamic perspective for understanding the effects of quantitative easing and tightening. For simplicity, let us consider a transitory supply shock in period 1 that is similar to QE, which is fully reversed in period 2 in a manner similar to QT. We plot the outstanding quantity of the bond available to the public in Figure (1), Panel q, which declines in period 1 due to QE and reverts to its pre-shock level in period 2 due to QT. The reversion in period 2 is anticipated when QE happens in period 1.

In the absence of portfolio frictions, the bond price goes up slightly in period 1 as the central bank purchases the bond, and it reverts very close to the pre-shock level in period 2 as the central bank exits the market. In this case, the bond price dynamics exhibit a simple inverted-V-shape, as represented by the blue line in Figure Notes: The left panel plots a transitory shock to the bond supply, which represents the central bank buying the bond in period 1 and selling it back in period 2. The right panel plots the bond price response. We consider three cases: without portfolio frictions, with portfolio frictions, and with portfolio frictions but keeping the long-term investors' wealth fixed. price adjustment in response to the quantity change is small. In the presence of portfolio frictions, this transitory supply shock could backfire and generate a novel overshooting pattern. In period 1, the bond demand becomes more inelastic: when the supply shock arrives, as the bond investors are reluctant to deviate from their prior portfolio shares in significant ways, they hold onto their bonds and crowd out the liquidity traders. Consequently, the liquidity traders hold a smaller quantity of bonds and demand a lower required return, which results in a higher bond price in period 1. Consistent with the findings in the literature, this inelastic demand curve allows QE to be effective in supporting the bond price.

However, when period 2 comes and the central bank unwinds its bond portfolio, the bond investors are starting from a lower bond position below their steady state. Their slow adjustment requires the liquidity traders to absorb the bonds offloaded by the central bank. Since the liquidity traders have a lower risk-taking capacity, they demand a higher expected return to hold more bonds, leading to a lower bond price which drops below the pre-shock level. In our calibration, the price drop in the QT period 2 is even greater than the price increase in the QE period 1, because it prices in the sum of higher expected returns required by the liquidity traders in all future periods in which they need to absorb the excess bond positions. In this way, QT generates a more complicated Sshape response in the bond price dynamics, as represented by the green line in Figure We can further decompose this overshooting effect in the bond price into two components. First, the direct effect is driven by the long-term bond investors' slow adjustment to their target portfolio share, which lowers bond demand following QT and reduces the bond price. Second, since the bond investors' portfolio is highly exposed to the bond price, the overshooting effect is amplified by an additional wealth effect: as the bond price drops following QT, the long-term bond investors' wealth declines and reduces their risk-taking capacity. This wealth effect creates a negative feedback loop that further depresses the bond price. The yellow line in Figure Quantitatively, our calibrated model implies that selling 7% of the outstanding Treasury debt as in the 2022-23 QT episode leads to a price decline of 5%. Du et al. (2024) focus on the bond yield responses during short announcement windows, and report that the cumulative announcement effect of the U.S. QT in 2022-23 is about 21 basis points on the 10-year bond yield and 19 basis points on the 30-year bond yield. These estimates correspond to roughly 2.1% and 5.7% decline in bond prices, respectively, which is consistent with our model's implication. That said, it is still possible that QT may have been partially anticipated and priced in by forward-looking investors.

As a result, part of the price decline may have happened before the announcement windows, which contributed to the dramatic bond price decline in this period. Moreover, the dynamic interaction between the two groups of investors also shapes the bond price response to cash flow shocks, which capture fiscal or fundamental shocks to the bond's real pay-off via either inflation or outright default. In our model, a positive cash flow shock is doubly good news because it not only raises the bond's pay-off but also lowers its discount rate. The discount rate effect is again due to the shock raising the bond investors' wealth, which allows them to take a greater bond position and crowd out the more risk-averse liquidity traders in this market. As the bond investors' wealth reverts to its steady-state level slowly over time, this discount rate effect can last longer than the underlying cash flow shock. Our model also generates other realistic features of bond pricing dynamics. For example, the yield spread between the long-term bond and the short rate predicts both future interest rates and bond risk premia. The predictability of risk premium is much stronger in the presence of portfolio frictions, as the cash flow and the supply shocks generate greater and more persistent effects on the long-term bond's required return in this case. Moreover, similar to models of financial intermediation that emphasize the importance of the financiers' net worth, in our model the bond investors' wealth emerges as a measure of the aggregate risk-taking capacity, which is negatively associated with the equilibrium bond risk premium.

In reality, central bank bond purchases and sales are (i) persistent and (ii) often announced well in advance. Is our result robust to these scenarios? In the first case, we examine a more persistent bond supply shock: after the central bank makes an unanticipated bond purchase today, it unwinds its position gradually over time. We find that a more gradual quantitative tightening policy can maintain the positive effect on the bond price upon bond purchase, while it alleviates the negative overshooting effect during the tightening phase by giving the long-term bond investors more time to adjust their portfolios. This result explains why central bank bond sales need to be slow and steady. However, this is not a free lunch: when the supply shock is persistent, bond investors experience a prolonged decline in wealth because the central bank's bond holding persistently depresses the return on the bond, which could reduce their risk-taking capacity if they also trade in other markets such as the corporate bonds and ABS markets. In the second case, we assume that the central bank announces a bond purchase that is scheduled to occur in a later period. We find that the bond price rises immediately upon receiving this news, as market participants anticipate the forthcoming supply shock and its positive impact on the bond price. As a result, forward guidance in the form of announcements of future bond purchases can proactively boost the bond price. However, as long as the bond purchase is quickly unwound, advance announcements do not alleviate the overshooting effect. This is because, despite the investors' anticipation of the event, they are unable to adjust their portfolios gradually in advance, because they need to accommodate the bond purchase in the QE phase in the first place.

In conclusion, we document changes in investor composition during the QT episodes in 2017-19 and 2022-23, which are accompanied by negative bond returns. Motivated by these empirical observations, we develop a general equilibrium model to study how investor heterogeneity and portfolio frictions generate a rich dynamic pattern for bond prices and portfolio holdings. Our model highlights a novel overshooting effect resulting from the dynamic interaction between different investor classes, which makes QT not merely QE in reverse mode. Our model remains simple and solvable as a linear equation system with forward-looking variables, which makes it easy to incorporate our mechanism into a DSGE framework and explore how the portfolio friction interacts with the real economy. We leave this path for future work. Literature. This paper contributes to our understanding of the effects of unconventional monetary policies. Building on the "portfolio rebalancing" channel that captures the direct effect of bond purchases on bond pricing, we develop a model to understand how investor heterogeneity and portfolio frictions shape the price dynamics (Tobin, 1958(Tobin, , 1969;;Vissing-Jorgensen and Krishnamurthy, 2011;Christensen and Rudebusch, 2012;Greenwood and Vayanos, 2014;Greenwood, Hanson, and Vayanos, 2016;Koijen, Koulischer, Nguyen, and Yogo, 2021;Vayanos and Vila, 2021). 1 The most related paper is Greenwood, Hanson, and Liao (2018), who study how portfolio frictions transmit the effect of quantitative easing to other asset classes. Building on this literature, we focus on how portfolio frictions break the symmetry between QE and QT and generate non-monotonic dynamics over time. 2 On the empirical side, Du, Forbes, and Luzzetti (2024) conduct a comprehensive empirical analysis of QT across developed countries. Consistent with our results, they also document that non-banks play an important role in absorbing the Treasury bonds sold by central banks. Moreover, D'Amico and Seida (2024) find that the Treasury yield sensitivity to QT surprises is larger than that to QE surprises, which is also consistent with our model's prediction. Du, Hébert, and Li (2023) also mention that dealers and hedge funds absorbed a large quantity of Treasury during QT1 in 2017-19.

Our model builds on heterogeneous-agent asset pricing models, which emphasize the heterogeneity in risk-taking capacity and in the access to financial markets (Chien, Cole, and Lustig, 2011;He and Krishnamurthy, 2013;Brunnermeier and Sannikov, 2014;Gabaix and Maggiori, 2015;Brunnermeier and Sannikov, 2016;Eisfeldt, Lustig, and Zhang, 2017;Haddad and Muir, 2021;Kekre, Lenel, and Mainardi, 2022). The most related paper is Chien et al. (2012), which examines how infrequent portfolio adjustment magnifies volatility. Our model studies the dynamic 1 Neely (2011); Bauer and Neely (2014); Greenwood, Hanson, Stein, and Sunderam (2020); Gourinchas, Ray, and Vayanos (2022); Jiang, Krishnamurthy, Lustig, and Sun (2021) study how the effects of quantitative easing on bond risk premia and convenience yields also impact the exchange rate dynamics. 2 Moreover, quantitative easing also impacts financial conditions by placing additional reserves on banks' balance sheets (Diamond, Jiang, and Ma, 2020;Copeland, Duffie, and Yang, 2021;Acharya, Chauhan, Rajan, and Steffen, 2022). The key message in our paper echoes this literature-the shrinkage of the central bank balance sheet may not be an entirely benign process. interaction between agents facing different frictions and risk-bearing capacity, which generates a novel overshooting pattern in bond price as the shock dissipates in the medium run. Our work is also related to the empirical literature on investor demand in the safe asset market, which also emphasizes the role of investor heterogeneity (Koijen and Yogo, 2020;Jiang et al., 2022a,b;Fang et al., 2022;Coppola, 2022;Eren et al., 2023;Zhou, 2023;Breckenfelder and De Falco, 2023).

Finally, we build on the literature on slow-moving capital (Mitchell et al., 2007;Brunnermeier and Nagel, 2008;Calvet et al., 2009;Duffie, 2010;Bilias et al., 2010;Ameriks and Zeldes, 2011), which, in our model, is generated by the portfolio adjustment cost. Gârleanu andPedersen (2013, 2016) examine this portfolio adjustment friction in a partial equilibrium portfolio choice model. 3We embed the implied portfolio choice decision in a general equilibrium model with heterogeneous agents to study the dynamic interaction between constrained and unconstrained agents.

We first document some new stylized facts about the change in investor composition during quantitative tightening. These results highlight the relevance of studying the heterogeneity in the investors' portfolio responses as a key to understand the pricing dynamics in the Treasury market, which we will use to motivate our heterogeneous-agent bond-pricing model in the subsequent section.

Investor Composition. We obtain data on the investor composition in the Treasury market from the Flow of Funds statistics, which breaks down the holdings of the U.S. government bills, notes and bonds by investor sectors such as pension funds, insurance companies, households, brokers and dealers, money market funds, and so on. We group these investors into four categories: (i) liquidity traders, (ii) long-term bond investors, (iii) the Federal Reserve (Fed), and (iv) the rest of the world. The liquidity traders are the financial intermediaries in the Treasury market that facilitate trades and seek short-term profit opportunities in this market, which include the brokers and dealers, banks (including credit unions and US depository institutes), and households. We include the household sector in the flow of flows because it includes hedge funds, private equity, and private trusts. There is evidence that the majority of the change in Treasury holdings by the household sector during QT episodes is driven by the hedge funds. We present the details in Appendix A.3. The long-term bond investors include all other domestic private sectors, including pension funds, insurance companies, ABS insurers, money market funds, ETFs, closed-end funds, mutual funds, government-sponsored enterprises, corporates, and holding companies. We typically think of these investors as the long-term holders of the Treasury debt who tend to trade less frequently. We do not include state and local governments, whose holdings we exclude from the total net supply. We include the Fed and the rest of the world as two separate categories. QT Episodes. We focus on two QT episodes and determine their beginning dates based on the FOMC meetings that first announced the start of the balance sheet normalization programs. The September 2017 FOMC meeting announced that QT1 will start in October 2017, and the May 2022 FOMC meeting announced that QT2 will start in June 2022. Hence, we assume that QT1 starts from 2017Q4, and QT2 starts from 2022Q2. p.t: Next, we zoom in on the two QT episodes and examine the change in investor composition during these episodes. In Figure (3), we plot the change in the holdings by each investor category scaled by the size of their holdings in the quarter prior to the QT episodes. Panel (a) plots the investor composition around QT1. As the Fed reduced its Treasury holdings starting from 2017Q4, the liquidity traders increased their holdings quickly. By 2019Q3, their holdings increased by 80%. In comparison, the bond investors and the rest of the world increased their positions at a much slower pace. Notes: We report the change in Treasury holdings scaled by the initial quantities prior to the QT episodes. The vertical black lines mark the beginning of the QT. The data are at quarterly frequency. Panel (b) plots the investor composition around QT2. Similarly, the reduction in the Fed's holdings was predominantly absorbed by the liquidity traders, who increased their holdings by 60% by 2023Q3. The bond investors increased their positions by less than 10%. Together, these patterns during QT episodes suggest that the liquidity traders-brokers and dealers, banks, and hedge funds-play an important role in absorbing the Fed's sales of the Treasury bonds. Although their holdings are small relative to the holdings by the bond investors and the rest of the world, they adjust their positions quickly and increase their positions by over 50% within one year. In other words, they bear a disproportionate amount of risk and imbalance during the QT episodes we study.

p.s: Changes in Investor Composition during QT Episodes
p.t: In Appendix A.4, we present more granular breakdowns of the investor composition within the categories of the liquidity traders and the bond investors. Brokers and dealers, banks, and hedge funds are the major investor classes within the liquidity trader category, and they all contributed to the fast increase in the liquidity traders' holdings. In Appendix A.5, we also conduct this analysis for the QE episodes. For the brokers and dealers who account for a major part of the liquidity traders, the patterns are symmetric: they quickly reduced their positions as the Federal Reserve bought the Treasury bonds. For the household sec-tor, their responses were consistent with the brokers and dealers in QE2 (2020-2022), but not in QE1 (2008)(2009)(2010)(2011)(2012)(2013). While the variations in the households' holdings were consistent with the available data on the hedge funds' holdings in QE2, we do not have data for QE1. It is possible that the households' holdings in QE1 were driven by other investor types. Finally, while our analysis focuses on the investors' asset holding in the Treasury debt market (the cash market), some investors are also active in the Treasury futures market. Liang (2024) shows that, while hedge funds took long positions on Treasury debt in the cash market, they also took short positions in the Treasury futures market. On the other hand, mutual funds and other asset managers took small positions in the cash market but large and positive positions in the futures market after QT. This pattern suggests that hedge funds acted like a pass-through between the cash and futures markets. They did not take large directional bets on Treasury debt, but instead did basis trades which exploited the price discrepancy between the two markets (Glicoes et al., 2024). In contrast, mutual funds and other asset managers provided liquidity indirectly by trading in the futures market, as their cash positions on Treasury debt were subject to leverage constraints.

p.s: Changes in Investor Composition during QT Episodes
p.t: Thus, if we jointly consider the Treasury cash and futures markets, we may need to classify mutual funds and other asset managers as liquidity traders as well. However, this modification does not affect our estimate of how much Treasury debt sold by the Fed was absorbed by the liquidity traders, since the indirect positions taken by asset managers in the futures market were already reflected in the direct positions taken by hedge funds in the cash market.

These patterns suggest that the shift in investor composition during the QT episodes coincided with a decline in bond price, especially during QT2. A natural question is whether the heterogeneity in investors' quantity responses contributed to the bond price decline. Empirically, it is difficult to identify the effect of QT, because demand shocks and monetary policy rates might be shifting at the same time. The QT events themselves could also contain information about other drivers of bond valuation. As a result, we turn to a theoretical approach in the next section to study how the changes in investor composition affect the valuation of the Treasury bonds.

Our empirical observations identify a class of investors-which we refer to as the liquidity traderswho respond quickly to the Fed's sales of the Treasury bonds and expand their Treasury holdings within a short period of time. In comparison, the bond investors who usually have a longer in-vestment horizon respond more slowly. Motivated by these observations, we develop a general equilibrium model of bond valuation with heterogeneous investors. We place an emphasis on how, in the presence of trading frictions, QT changes the composition of the marginal investors in the market and as a result affects the valuation of the Treasury bonds.

We consider a simple market economy with two financial assets. One asset, referred to as the reserve, is a one-period bond with a risk-free interest rate i t . This asset represents the interestbearing reserve. As the central bank stands ready to buy or sell the reserve at the given interest rate i t , we assume that it has a perfectly elastic supply. The other asset, which we refer to as the (long-term) bond, is a perpetual bond that pays a time-varying coupon in each period. In period t, the ex-coupon bond price is denoted by p t , and the bond pays a stochastic coupon denoted by x t . This asset represents the government's longterm debt liabilities. While most government debt promises a fixed nominal payoff, its real value may vary and render the debt risky in real terms. The stochastic payoff could also be interpreted as capturing government default or variations in the fiscal conditions (Jiang et al., 2019). 4 For concreteness, we adopt the inflation interpretation. Then, we can think of the steady-state value x as capturing the promised nominal payoff, and the deviation x t -x as the variations in the real cash flow due to inflation. The cum-coupon holding period return of the bond is defined as The bond supply is denoted by q t . We assume that the bond coupon x t , the bond quantity q t , and the reserve interest rate i t are exogenously given. The bond coupon reflects the fundamental shocks to the government debt, the bond quantity reflects the government's issuance decision as well as the central bank's quantity-based monetary policy, and the reserve interest rate reflects the central bank's conventional monetary policy.

There are two types of investors. Both take prices as given. We assume that one type of investors is a more natural holder of risky assets because they have a lower risk aversion. However, they cannot always hold as much risky asset as they desire because they face trading frictions. The other type of investors charges a higher premium for holding risky assets, but they stand ready to absorb the excess amount of risky assets without trading frictions. For stationarity, we assume an overlapping generations (OLG) structure for both types of investors. Bond Investors. The first type is bond investors, who allocate their portfolio between the perpetual bond and the reserve. They live for one period and inherit some wealth from the previous generation. The portfolio shares that a bond investor allocates to the perpetual bond and reserve are z t and 1 -z t , respectively. Then, the investor's portfolio return in period t + 1 can be written In period t, the investor's objective is to choose the portfolio allocation to maximize the expected excess return adjusted by risks and trading costs. The objective function is where γ is bond investor's risk-aversion coefficient, and σ 2 t = var t (r t+1 ) is the conditional variance of the bond return. This objective function can be motivated by the optimization problem of an investor who has a power utility over wealth in the next period, and faces a transaction cost that directly lowers the portfolio return. We present this derivation in Appendix B.1.

The trading cost function c(z t ; z t-1 , z) is defined as which assumes that the bond investors face two types of costs. First and foremost, they are penalized for changing their portfolio weight z t relative to the last period's value z t-1 . This is the key friction that generates our main results. Second, the bond investors are also penalized for deviating from the benchmark portfolio allocation z, which can be motivated by the investors' desire to stay close to a benchmark portfolio. This assumption does not affect the qualitative response of the bond price to shocks, but it produces quantitatively more realistic dynamics in the medium run. We pick a small η = 0.1, so that the trading costs are mainly driven by rebalancing the portfolio weight relative to the last period's value. The trading cost is scaled by the asset return variance σ 2 t following Gârleanu and Pedersen (2013). Denote the bond's excess return as Then, the first-order condition with respect to z t implies the following solution for the optimal portfolio weight z t : which is a weighted average between E t [er t+1 ]/(γσ 2 t ), the standard mean-variance solution for a one-period investor, and (ηz t-1 + (1 -η)z), the reference portfolio determined by the previous period's portfolio weight z t-1 and the benchmark portfolio allocation z.

In Appendix C.3, we consider a more general case in which the bond investors have an infinite horizon. In this case, when they decide their portfolio allocation, they take into account not only how the current portfolio deviates from the previous position, but also how it affects the transaction costs arising from future portfolio adjustments. This additional consideration effectively makes the investors even more reluctant to deviate from the given path of portfolio allocation, which further lowers the demand elasticity in a way similar to increasing the trading cost parameter µ. Quantitatively, our results remain robust to this extension. As such, we stick to the baseline model which has a simpler algebraic solution and more intuitive interpretation. Finally, let w t denote the bond investors' wealth. We assume its law of motion follows an autoregressive process: which introduces a bequest motive to ensure stationarity in a simple way. Specifically, the bond investors of generation t receive a fixed endowment w e and also inherit part of the wealth from the previous generation t-1. The previous generation t-1 bequeaths a fraction ϕ of their wealth to the next generation, and consumes the remaining wealth. In this way, after many generations following an initial shock, the bond investors' wealth will return to a steady-state level w in expectation.

The second class of investors is the liquidity traders, with a constant mass of m. They also face the mean-variance trade-off over their portfolio return, but they do not pay the transaction cost that the bond investors do. These liquidity traders take a zero-cost longshort position on the bond versus the reserve. Let ℓ t denote their holdings of the bond, and -ℓ t denote their holdings of the reserve. The return on their portfolio in period t + 1 is given by At time t, liquidity trader's objective is to choose their portfolio allocation in bond, ℓ t , to maximize the present value of expected excess returns, penalized for risks. where ω is the risk aversion coefficient of the liquidity traders. We assume that the liquidity traders are more risk-averse than the bond investors, i.e., γ < ω, so the bond has to offer a higher risk premium if it is held by the liquidity traders as opposed to the bond investors. Solving the first-order condition with respect to ℓ t , we obtain the following solution for their optimal portfolio choice ℓ t : These liquidity traders play similar roles as the arbitrageurs in the preferred habitat models (Vayanos and Vila, 2021). However, unlike the preferred habitat investors in such models, the longterm bond investors in our model do not have a fixed habitat, and instead optimize their portfolio composition subject to trading frictions. As a result, our model generates richer predictions for the short-run and long-run elasticities of bond demand.

Alternatively, Gabaix and Maggiori (2015) provides a different microfoundation, in which these liquidity traders are risk-neutral but face a financial friction that is increasing in the variance of the risky asset's return. Regardless of the microfoundation, these liquidity traders absorb excess positions, both positive and negative, in the bond market from the bond investors as well as the government sector, and they charge a risk premium for providing this service. Their optimality condition implies a tight link between their portfolio position ℓ t and the bond's discount rate E t [er t+1 ], which will be the key to understand the equilibrium outcomes as we next discuss. The Government and the Central Bank. Besides the two types of private investors, there is a government sector who controls the aggregate supply of the bond. We model its action as an exogenous policy. The government issues and retires the perpetual bond over time. Let q gov t denote the quantity outstanding in period t. The government's budget constraint is (p t + x t )q gov t-1 = s t + p t q gov t , where the left-hand side captures what the government owes and the right-hand side captures its primary surplus s t and the proceeds from new issuances of the bond. Moreover, the central bank can also buy and sell the perpetual bond. Let q cb t denote the quantity held by the central bank. Then, the total amount of the bond available to private investors can be written as q t = q gov t -q cb t .

While the magnitude of this friction is greater than the typical level of transaction costs in the Treasury market, we interpret the portfolio friction more broadly as the combination of various frictions that prevent the bond investors from fully rebalancing their portfolio. The Cash Flow Shock. First, we plot the impulse responses to a positive shock to the bond's cash flow x t in Figure (C.5). The top panels report the dynamics of the bond valuation, including its cash flow x t , ex-coupon price p t , cum-coupon return r t , and expected excess return E t [er t+1 ]. The bottom panels report the dynamics of investors' holdings and wealth, including the bond investors' wealth w t , their portfolio share in the bond z t , their bond holding in dollar value w t z t , and the liquidity traders' holding in dollar value mℓ t . In this plot, the shock is transitory: the cash flow x t increases in period 1 and reverts to the steady-state value in period 2. We consider two variants of the model: one in which the bond investors do not face the transaction cost (µ = 0), and one in which the bond investors face a transaction cost (µ = 150). We begin by noting the similarities between the two model variants. A high cash flow x t in period 1 raises the bond's cum-coupon return r t in period 1, which increases the bond investors' wealth w t as they hold a considerable share of the bond in their portfolio. As the bond investors become wealthier, they hold a higher dollar amount w t z t of the bond, even if the share of their wealth z t allocated to the bond remains the same or, as the figure shows, declines slightly due to a lower expected bond return. Given a constant bond supply, this increase in the bond investors' holdings crowds out the liquidity traders' holdings of the bond mℓ t , leading the liquidity traders to hold a smaller quantity of bond and require a lower bond risk premium for compensation in equilibrium.

In this sense, a positive cash flow shock is doubly good news for the bond market: it not only raises the cash flow, but also lowers the discount rate, which further boosts the bond valuation. 6 For the convenience of discussion, we also introduce the bond yield y t defined as the yield-to-maturity evaluated at the steady-state (nominal) cash flows, which solves p t = ∞ h=1 x/(y t ) h . Conversely, a negative cash flow shock is doubly bad news, as it not only reduces the cash flow but also raises the discount rate. Moreover, beyond period 2, as the bond investors' wealth is a persistent state variable, their bond holdings w t z t in dollar value remain high and continue to crowd out the liquidity traders' positions. As a result, the bond valuation remains high even after the direct cash-flow effect of the transitory shock disappears. The two model variants also have important differences. If the bond investors face a transaction cost, when the bond's expected return declines in period 1, they become less willing to lower their portfolio share z t allocated to the bond. As a result, the portfolio share z t declines less upon the shock's arrival in the µ = 150 case relative to the µ = 0 case. This sluggish portfolio adjustment implies that the bond investors hold more bond w t z t when the shock arrives, which further crowds Notes: This figure reports the responses of the key state variables to a transitory shock to the bond's cash flow. out the liquidity traders and leads to more dramatic responses in the bond price and the bond's expected return. In this way, the presence of portfolio friction makes the bond valuation more sensitive to the cash flow shock. The Bond Quantity Shock. Next, we consider a transitory reduction in bond quantity q t available to the public in period 1. As we discussed in the model setup, this shock can come from either a surprise reduction in government debt issuance, or bond purchase by the central bank. For the sake of discussion, we interpret this shock as central bank bond purchase. More precisely, since the bond quantity reverts to the steady-state level in period 2, this shock represents a transitory quantitative easing that is immediately unwound in the following period. We report the impulse responses in the same format in Figure Notes: This figure reports the responses of the key state variables to a transitory shock to the bond supply. We consider two cases: with and without transaction costs. The frictionless case with µ = 0 presents a simple story. As the bond quantity shrinks in period 1, the bond price p t goes up, and the bond investors become more wealthy. Both the bond investors and the liquidity traders lower their holdings of the bond as the total supply shrinks, which generates a reduction in the discount rate that is consistent with the price increase. In period 2, as the supply shock dissipates, the bond price falls back and the bond return turns negative. This negative return generates a slight loss in the bond investors' wealth, which takes a few more periods to recover. In this way, the price response has a simple inverted-V shape that first goes up in the QE phase and then goes down in the QT phase.

The case with the transaction cost (i.e., µ = 150) has much richer dynamics. Upon the arrival of the negative supply shock, the bond investors again have sluggish adjustment in their portfolio choice z t and hold onto more bond, which requires the liquidity traders to sell more bond in equilibrium. As the liquidity traders require a lower expected return, the bond price p t increases more in period 1. In other words, the portfolio friction makes the investors' demand more inelastic in the short run. Quantitatively, a 5% reduction in the bond quantity raises the bond price by about 1.5%, implying a demand elasticity of 3.3, which is consistent with the estimate Koijen and Yogo (2020) obtains in a global asset demand system. Surprisingly, unlike the µ = 0 case, the bond price does not revert to the steady-state level when the supply shock dissipates in period 2. Instead, the bond price experiences a significant drop below the steady-state level. To understand this result, we note that the quantitative easing lowers the bond investors' portfolio share z t in period 1, which is sticky due to the portfolio friction. When the supply shock dissipates, the bond investors' bond holding z t remains low. As a result, the liquidity traders have to hold more bonds from period 2 onwards, which raises the required discount rate and lowers the bond price below the steady-state value. Quantitatively, this "overshooting" effect lowers the bond price by 2% below the steady state in period 2, which is even stronger than the supply shock's immediate positive effect in period 1. The key intuition is that the bond price is forward-looking: its response to the supply shock depends not only on how the shock affects the discount rate today, but also on how it affects the discount rates in future periods. For example, in period 2, investors expect not only a higher bond discount rate E 2 [er 3 ] today due to the liquidity traders' higher bond holdings, but also higher discount rates in future periods as this situation persists. As a result, the response of the period-2 bond price is greater than the response of the period-2 discount rate, which temporarily lowers the bond price below the long-run level in a fashion similar to Dornbusch (1976) in the context of exchange rate dynamics.

Moreover, this result offers a reason why it is a natural benchmark for the central bank to purchase the entire new bond issuance in crisis periods. The key is to modulate how much debt the liquidity traders have to absorb. Suppose the bond investors remain completely inactive. Then, a central bank bond purchase equal to the net issuance amount prevents the liquidity traders from absorbing additional bond positions and charging a higher discount rate. When the fundamental of the bond deteriorates and the bond investors are also reducing their bond positions, the central bank needs to purchase more than the issuance amount to absorb the additional supply from the market and prevent the bond price from going down, a pattern we observed during the Covid-19 crisis period. Isolate the Wealth Effect. We find it useful to additionally consider a case which mutes the wealth effect, which is presented in Appendix C.1 in detail. In this case, we assume that the bond investors' wealth is fixed at the steady-state level, which allows us to isolate the direct effect of the supply shock from the amplifying effect due to the its impact on the long-term bond investors' wealth and hence their risk-taking capacity. Consider the same transitory bond supply shock that reduces the quantity of the publicly available long-term bond. As the central bank offloads the purchased bond in the QT phase, the bond price drops and lowers the bond investors' wealth due to their portfolio exposure. This wealth effect in turn reduces the bond investors' risk-taking capacity and their demand for the bond, which further lowers the bond price and creates a negative feedback loop. We find this wealth effect to be quantitatively important in our model. As shown in Figure (C.6), it explains over half of the bond price drop in the QT phase. Interestingly, the wealth effect is also asymmetric between the QE and QT phases: the bond price increase in the QE phase is similar in magnitude with and without the wealth effect, as it is driven by the direct effect of the supply shock. In contrast, the bond price drop in the QT phase is much larger with the wealth effect.

The importance of this wealth effect reminds us of the banking crisis in early 2023, which was accompanied by mark-to-market losses on the U.S. banks' bond portfolios due to rising interest rates. The wealth effect we highlight in this section suggests that the reduction in the long-term investors' risk-taking capacity could also be a main contributor to the long-term bond price decline in this episode, as it can make the bond price even more sensitive to shocks. In this simulated sample, we also consider two standard regressions involving the bond's yield spread, defined as y t -i t . First, we regress the change in the interest rate on the reserve on the yield spread: This regression captures the extent to which the long-term bond yield prices in the expected path of future short-term interest rates. We refer to the regression coefficient β IE as the interest rate expectations (IE) coefficient. Under the expectation hypothesis, β IE should be positive. However, in this case with no variation in the short rate, we find that β IE is zero. Moreover, we regress the bond's excess return on the yield spread: This regression captures the extent to which the long-term bond yield forecasts the bond's future excess return (Fama and Bliss, 1987). We refer to the regression coefficient β RP as the return predictability (RP) coefficient. Consistent with the finding in the literature, the yield spread captures the bond's risk premium, and we find a positive β RP . Moreover, in the presence of the transaction cost, β RP is higher, implying a greater time variation in the bond's risk premium. In Column (2), we consider the bond's supply shock alone. In this case, the transaction cost raises the bond return volatility from 0.4% to 5% per annum, which demonstrates the importance of the transaction cost in amplifying the bond's return volatility. The supply shock also generates a very large RP coefficient, suggesting that the central bank's bond supply policy can be very effective in influencing the bond's pricing and risk premium.

In this section, we consider two forms of debt supply management, which are (1) a surprise central bank bond purchase that unwinds slowly over time, and ( 2) an announcement of central bank bond purchase that takes place in a later period. p.s: Gradual Tightening in the Presence of Slow-Moving Capital
p.t: Quantitative easing has become an important tool to support the bond price and lower the long-term interest rate amidst recessions and crises. Our results above suggest that a transitory quantitative easing that unwinds too quickly generates an overshooting effect that worsens the price drop once the supply shock dissipates. In this section, we discuss whether a more gradual tightening strategy generates different effects. We consider a simple AR(1) family of bond supply shocks, which corresponds to different θ q coefficients in the specification of the exogenous supply process, reproduced below, We choose θ q = {0, 0.5, 0.80, 0.90, 0.95}, which implies half-lives of {0, 1, 3.1, 6.6, 13.5} years. Figure ( 9) reports the impulse responses under transaction costs (i.e., µ = 150). We find that, as we make the bond supply shock more persistent, the increase in period-1 bond price becomes stronger, and the overshooting effect in subsequent periods becomes weaker. Both patterns can be explained by the following intuition: as the central bank quits quantitative easing more gradually, the bond investors have more time to adjust their portfolio holdings and hence behave more similarly to the frictionless case. As a result, the liquidity traders are not required to absorb more bonds from period 2 onwards, leading to a persistent decrease in the bond's discount rate which raises the bond price across all periods. Under our calibration, when the persistence parameter is Notes: This figure reports the responses of the key state variables to a family of bond supply shocks. p.t: θ q = 0.95, which implies a half-life of 13.5 years, the bond price never drops below its steady-state level, implying that the quantitative easing only has positive effects on the bond price. Does the Fed conduct QT slow enough to be consistent with this case? Our empirical analysis suggests that the liquidity traders' bond positions increased dramatically and much more than other investors after QT announcements, which is inconsistent with a persistent decline in their bond positions as predicted by our model with more persistent QT. As such, QT in the U.S. may have been conducted faster than the long-term bond investors' portfolio adjustment speed, which could have generated the overshooting effect. Moreover, we also note that, while a persistent supply shock keeps the bond price above the steady-state value throughout the QT episode, it is not a free lunch: it also lowers the bond in-vestors' wealth w t for an extended period of time. This is because this shock supports bond price by persistently lowering the realized returns from holding the bond. Since the bond investors hold the bond with a leverage, their wealth is persistently depressed. As such, if they are also active marginal investors in other asset markets such as the corporate bond market, then, this wealth effect could reduce their risk-taking capacity and raise the risk premium in other asset markets.

p.s: Impulse Responses to Shocks to Expectations
p.t: We also consider a shock to the expectation of the bond supply, which could be interpreted as a form of forward guidance. To make the figures easier to read, we assume that the news arrives in period 1 which announces a change in the bond supply in period 5. We report the impulse responses in Figure (10). For simplicity, we only include the bond quantity q t , ex-coupon price p t , expected excess return E t [er t+1 ], and the bond investors' portfolio share in the bond z t . We report the full impulse responses in Appendix C.2. In period 5, when the shock is realized, the bond quantity declines by 5% and, as the investors have downward-sloping demand curves, the bond price goes up. In anticipation of the higher price in period 5, the bond price also increases once the news arrives in period 1. In other words, This expected quantity shock also generates the overshooting pattern that we discussed in the benchmark case in Figure (6). In the presence of portfolio friction (i.e., µ = 150), as the bond quantity reverts to the steady-state level in period 6, the bond investors' portfolio share z t remains low. As a result, the liquidity traders have to absorb additional bond shares and require a higher discount rate, leading to a subsequent drop in the bond price. In this case, even though the bond investors have prior knowledge of the scheduled central bank bond sale, they cannot adjust their portfolio gradually towards the desired position in advance. This is because the required adjustment in QT period 6 is relative to the change in the portfolio share in QE period 5. Before the QE happens and lowers the bond investors' portfolio share, their portfolio share stays close to the desired level and has no reason to adjust.

This paper develops a simple framework for understanding bond price dynamics in the presence of slow-moving capital. It highlights a novel overshooting effect that negatively impacts the longterm bond price when quantitative tightening is conducted too fast. As a result, due to the portfolio friction, quantitative tightening is not simply a reversal of quantitative easing. We also examine the change in investor composition during two QE episodes. The first one (QE1) spans from November 2008 to June 2013. On November 25, 2008, Ben Bernanke announced the initiation of a program aimed at purchasing the direct obligations of housing-related governmentsponsored enterprises. Later, on June 19, 2013, Bernanke announced a gradual reduction, commonly referred to as "tapering," of some of the Fed's QE policies, contingent upon continued positive economic data. Within this time frame, there were three rounds of QE, commencing in November 2008, November 2010, and September 2012. The second one (QE2) spans from March 2020 to May 2022, which precedes QT2 which we study in the main text. However, the domestic household sector increased their holdings while the Fed was also buying bonds during QE1, whereas they decreased their holdings during QE2. While we do not have further breakdown of the transactions by the household sector, it is possible that the bond purchases during QE1 were not made by the hedge funds, but by other investor types categorized under the household sector which might be best not classified as liquidity traders. In comparison, as we discussed in Section A.3, data on the hedge funds' Treasury holdings during QE2 are available, and they are consistent with the household sector's holdings in this episode. Overall, the brokers and dealers acted in a way consistent with our view of the liquidity traders, who absorbed the imbalances created by the Federal Reserve's purchases and sales. The household sector had different reactions in the two episodes, which might be due to different types of investors within this sector. It is also important to note that there was another major seller of the Treasury bonds during both QE episodes: the government issuer itself. As such, the Fed's purchase of the Treasury bonds during QE do not necessarily mean that the private investors have to lower their holdings. We consider two cases: with and without transaction costs. The Bond Quantity Shock. The impulse responses to the transitory bond quantity shock are similar to the results in the main text qualitatively, but there are some quantitative differences. First, the initial bond price increase in response to QE in period 1 is stronger, implying an even lower demand elasticity of 1.9 instead of 3.3 from the main text. Second, the price overshoot in period 2 is smaller in magnitude. The intuition is that, as the bond investors have a longer horizon, they understand that if they lower their bond share in period 1 during the QE phase, they need to buy back more bonds and incur greater transaction costs in period 2 during the QT phase. This makes them even more reluctant to adjust their bond holdings in period 1. As a result, when QT happens in period 2, the liquidity traders need to absorb fewer bonds sold by the central bank, leading to a smaller price decline.
